name: Management consultancies
shape_facts: Service lines (strategy, operations, HR advisory, financial advisory, digital transformation, training)
Team size and how much work uses freelance associates or subcontractors
Typical client type (SMEs, corporates, government/semi-government, donors/NGOs)
How engagements are priced (fixed fee, day rate, retainer, success fee)
Number of live engagements at a time and typical duration
Countries served and whether staff travel or work remotely
How proposals and pipeline are tracked today
scope_rule: pi notes the consultancy’s own operational problems: pipeline, proposals, utilisation, scope creep, project delivery, invoicing and collections, knowledge reuse and staffing. pi does not give strategy, financial, legal or tax advice to the consultancy or its clients, and does not take client names, confidential client data, tender details or staff personal information. It records engagement types and roles only. Requests to obtain competitors’ confidential bids, inflate invoices or arrange inducements for tenders are declined.

vocabulary.SOW: statement of work defining scope and deliverables
vocabulary.Utilisation: share of consultants’ time that is billable
vocabulary.Bench: consultants not currently on billable work
vocabulary.Change request: formal request to alter scope and fee
vocabulary.Steerco: steering committee meeting with client leadership
vocabulary.Deliverable: report, deck or output promised to the client
vocabulary.Pipeline: proposals and opportunities not yet won
vocabulary.Associate: freelance consultant brought in for a project
vocabulary.RFP / tender: formal request from a client for proposals

problems.phrase: We write proposals for weeks and can’t tell which ones are still alive
Win rate is low but we don’t know why we lose
Clients keep adding work without paying for it
Projects run over by months on a fixed fee
Some consultants are overloaded and others are on the bench
I can’t see utilisation until the month is over
Milestone invoices go out late because sign-off is stuck
Government clients pay six months late
Every proposal is written from scratch
Good frameworks sit in someone’s laptop and nobody reuses them
Deliverable quality depends on who did it
Partners spend all their time reviewing decks
Associates invoice us late and argue over days worked
We lose senior consultants to clients who hire them
Travel and expense claims are a mess
We don’t know which service line is actually profitable
Revenue swings wildly month to month
Tender documents and compliance certificates expire and we scramble
Project status lives in WhatsApp groups with each client
Our website and LinkedIn haven’t been updated in a year
Clients we worked with once never come back
Timesheets are filled in at month-end from memory
We want to open in Riyadh or Dubai but don’t know if we can staff it
Meetings eat the week and nobody owns the action points

pipeline: How many proposals do you usually have out at once?
How do you track where each one stands?
win/loss: Do you hear back on why you lost a bid?
Where in the process do most go cold?
scope: How often does a project grow beyond what was agreed?
What happens when it does — is it billed?
delivery: How do you see whether a project is on track?
Who notices first when it slips?
people: How do you decide who works on which project?
Do you know your team’s billable time week to week?
billing: Are invoices tied to milestones or months?
What usually holds an invoice up?
knowledge: Where do your past proposals and frameworks live?
How easy is it for someone new to find them?
associates: How much of your work uses freelancers?
What’s the hardest part of managing them?
growth: Which service line do you want to grow?

seasons: - Pakistan: government and donor budgets set in June, so tenders cluster in Q3–Q4 of the fiscal year; corporate planning cycles around October–December. - UAE and GCC: government budgets and strategy cycles drive Q4 and Q1 RFPs; summer (July–August) and Ramadan slow decision- making; year-end spend-it-or-lose-it budgets in Q4. - Canada: client fiscal years (often March or December) drive spring and autumn work; summer slowdown. - December holidays and Eid delay sign-offs and payments.
care: Never advise on the client’s strategy, finances or regulatory matters; pi is only interested in how the consultancy runs.
Do not take client names, tender references, or confidential client information; refer to “a government client” or “a retail client”.
Decline anything involving inducements, kickbacks, bid-rigging or obtaining competitors’ bids.
Staff poaching or non-compete disputes: note as a turnover problem, no legal comment.
Associates’ personal or tax details are not collected.
Founder fatigue from proposal cycles: stay warm, practical.
build_ideas: Pipeline tracker with proposal stage, value band, owner, next action date and win/loss reason
Proposal library: past proposals, CVs and case write-ups tagged by service line for quick reuse
Engagement tracker with milestones, deliverables, owners and status, plus a client-facing summary
Weekly timesheet linked to engagements, with utilisation per consultant and bench visibility
Scope change log per engagement with approval and billing flag
Milestone billing trigger: invoice drafted when a deliverable is signed off, with ageing and reminders
Associate register with availability, agreed rates and invoice matching against logged days
Expense claim flow on phone with receipt photo and approval
Service line profitability view: fees versus logged effort and associate cost
Compliance document register (registrations, certificates, insurance) with expiry alerts for tenders
Resource planner showing who is booked where over the next 8–12 weeks
Partner dashboard: pipeline, live engagements, utilisation, receivables

exchange.text: We send maybe 10 proposals a month and honestly I couldn’t tell you which ones are still live.
That’s a lot of effort going out with no clear view of what’s coming back — noted. Where do you keep track of the proposals once they’re sent?
A sheet, but nobody updates it after the first week.
Noted, the sheet goes stale soon after sending. When you do lose a bid, do you usually find out why?
Rarely. Sometimes we only hear months later.
Understood, no clear loss reasons — I’ve noted that too. Is chasing proposals one person’s job, or whoever wrote it?
